mean: full of too many people
ex: The Dadar platform was so crowded at nine that Rohan let two locals leave without him.
ex2: Grandpa refused to go to the crowded Sunday market, so Kavya ordered the vegetables on her phone instead.
note: Say 'The bus was crowded', not 'There was rush'. 'Rush' for a crowd is Indian English; elsewhere 'rush' means hurry.

mean: calm and quiet, with no noise or trouble
ex: After the noise of the Varanasi ghats, the early morning boat ride felt strangely peaceful.
ex2: Once the wedding guests had left, the Ludhiana house felt peaceful for the first time in a week.

mean: a little wet, in an unpleasant way
ex: By August the walls of our Kochi flat were damp, and every leather bag grew green mould.
ex2: Sanjay's cricket whites were still damp after a rainy day at the nets, so he hung them under the fan.
note: Damp is usually unpleasant; 'moist' is neutral or pleasant, as in a moist cake.

mean: weak and hard to see, hear or smell
ex: From the hostel terrace we heard the faint sound of a shehnai from a wedding three lanes away.
ex2: There was a faint smell of gas in the Pune kitchen, so Aditi opened every window and called the agency.
note: Also a verb: to faint is to fall unconscious. 'I haven't the faintest idea' means no idea at all.

mean: small from side to side; not wide
ex: In the narrow lanes of Chandni Chowk, a cycle rickshaw and a cow cannot pass each other.
ex2: The road to the Himachal village was so narrow that our driver had to reverse whenever a truck came down.
note: 'A narrow escape' means you only just escaped; 'narrow-minded' means not open to new ideas.

mean: busy and full of people moving about
ex: Crawford Market is bustling by seven, with porters shouting and mango sellers calling out prices.
ex2: By Diwali week, the tiny Indore sweet shop is bustling, with three extra counters and a queue on the pavement.
note: The t is silent: BUS-ling. Bustling sounds lively and positive; 'crowded' can sound uncomfortable.

mean: calm, peaceful and untroubled
ex: As our houseboat drifted through the Kerala backwaters at dawn, the water lay serene and still.
ex2: The marble walkway around the Golden Temple's pool feels serene at four in the morning, before the crowds arrive.
note: Works for people too: 'She stayed serene while the wedding guests argued.'

mean: too small for the people or things inside it
ex: Six of us shared one cramped room in a Mukherjee Nagar PG while preparing for the civil services exam.
ex2: Our cramped Bengaluru office had twelve desks in a room meant for six, so we took our calls on the stairs.
note: Cramped describes a space; crowded describes too many people. A room for two can feel cramped.

mean: dark and dull, or sad and without hope
ex: The sky over Shillong stayed gloomy for a week, and even the market sellers seemed low.
ex2: The hospital corridor in Patna was long and gloomy, lit by a single flickering tube light.
note: Works for weather, rooms and moods: a gloomy sky, a gloomy corridor, a gloomy prediction.

mean: having a sweet, pleasant smell
ex: Flower sellers outside Madurai's Meenakshi temple string fragrant jasmine into thick garlands.
ex2: Nani's kitchen in Lucknow is fragrant with saffron and cardamom whenever she cooks biryani for Eid.
note: Only for pleasant smells. For strong smells use 'pungent'; for bad ones, 'foul'.

mean: with a lot of water in the air, so you feel hot and sticky
ex: Mumbai in June is so humid that a fresh shirt sticks to your back before you reach the station.
ex2: The dressing room at the Chennai stadium was so humid that the players' kits never dried between sessions.
note: The noun is 'humidity', not 'humidness'. Delhi's May heat is dry; Chennai's is humid.

mean: completely confused, with no order at all
ex: The Kashmere Gate bus stand was chaotic: conductors shouting, buses reversing, and nobody sure which queue was which.
ex2: The kitchen was chaotic on the morning of the wedding, with three cooks, two aunts and one tiny stove.
note: The 'ch' is a k sound, as in chemistry: KAY-oss, kay-OT-ik.

mean: very bright and strong, or very clear in the mind
ex: Ammamma still has vivid memories of the snake-boat races she watched as a girl in Alappuzha.
ex2: The back of the truck was painted in vivid pinks and greens, with 'Horn OK Please' in big yellow letters.
note: Used for colours, dreams and memories. A 'vivid imagination' easily pictures things that are not there.

mean: dark and dirty, hard to see through; or unclear and dishonest
ex: After the floods the Yamuna ran murky brown, carrying plastic and broken branches past the ghats.
ex2: Nobody wanted to swim in the murky village pond after the buffaloes had spent the whole afternoon in it.
note: Also figurative: 'the murky world of land deals' means hidden and probably dishonest.

mean: having a very strong, sharp smell or taste
ex: The pungent smell of mustard oil smoking in the kadhai made everyone in the Kolkata kitchen sneeze.
ex2: At the Bhubaneswar fish market, the pungent smell of dried fish reached us before we even saw the stalls.
note: Not always bad: garlic, hing and mustard are pungent. For a bad smell, use 'foul' or 'stinking'.

mean: thick, green and full of healthy plants
ex: After the first monsoon showers, the tea gardens of Munnar turn lush and almost glow.
ex2: The cricket ground in Dharamshala has a lush outfield, with snowy peaks rising behind the stands.
note: Lush suggests thick, rich growth; 'green' alone only names the colour.

mean: old, broken and in very bad condition because nobody cared for it
ex: The dilapidated haveli in Jaipur still had painted ceilings, though pigeons nested in its broken jharokhas.
ex2: The dilapidated village school building was finally repaired after the parents wrote to the district collector.
note: For buildings, vehicles and furniture, not people.

mean: so hot that you feel uncomfortable and sweaty
ex: On the sweltering May afternoon, the whole Nagpur colony hid indoors with the coolers running.
ex2: After a sweltering day of Test cricket in Chennai, the bowlers went straight into ice baths.
note: Sweltering suggests heavy, sweaty heat; 'scorching' suggests a burning sun.

mean: empty, lonely and without life or comfort
ex: Beyond the last village, the white salt flats of the Rann of Kutch stretch silent and desolate for miles.
ex2: After the last train left, the small Rajasthan station looked desolate, with one dog asleep on the platform.
note: Can describe a person too: feeling desolate means feeling deeply alone and sad.

mean: perfectly clean and untouched, as if new
ex: The beach on Havelock Island was pristine: no plastic, no hawkers, only turtle tracks in the sand.
ex2: Dadi's Kanjeevaram saree, wrapped in muslin for forty years, was still in pristine condition.
note: A pristine forest is untouched by people; a pristine shirt is spotless.

mean: showing great wealth; very rich and grand
ex: The wedding hall in Hyderabad was opulent, with crystal chandeliers, silver thalis and walls of fresh roses.
ex2: The Mysore Palace is opulent, with gold-painted pillars, carved doors and enormous chandeliers.
note: Can sound admiring or slightly critical, hinting at too much display of money.

mean: badly made and looking ready to fall apart
ex: A ramshackle bus with a cracked windscreen carried us up the mountain road to Tawang.
ex2: Behind the stadium, a ramshackle tea stall of tin sheets and bamboo served the best cutting chai in Guwahati.
note: Ramshackle means badly built; dilapidated means once fine, now ruined by neglect.

mean: a loud mix of harsh, clashing sounds
ex: Horns, temple bells and a loudspeaker selling onions made a cacophony at the Lucknow crossing.
ex2: When the power came back, the hostel woke to a cacophony of fans, ringing phones and twenty alarms.
note: Stress the second syllable: kuh-KOF. Its opposite is 'harmony'.

mean: peaceful and beautiful, like a perfect picture
ex: Their idyllic Coorg homestay had coffee bushes, a little stream and no mobile signal at all.
ex2: For Simran, growing up among the apple orchards of a Himachal village felt idyllic, until she needed fast internet for college.
note: Also said eye-DIL-ik. Often hints that real life is less perfect than the picture.

mean: green and covered with grass and plants
ex: The train wound through the verdant hills of the Western Ghats, with a waterfall on every slope.
ex2: After a good monsoon, the verdant paddy fields of Thanjavur stretched all the way to the horizon.
note: A literary word for writing; in speech, 'green' or 'lush' sounds more natural.

mean: the earthy smell when rain falls on dry ground
ex: When the first monsoon rain hit the dusty Jodhpur courtyard, the petrichor drew the whole family outside.
ex2: Sitting in her Bengaluru office, Neha smelt the petrichor through the open window and knew the rain had come.
note: Scientists coined it in 1964. Kannauj perfumers bottle the same smell as 'mitti attar'.

mean: making a lot of loud sound
ex: Our flat faces a noisy main road, so Papa sleeps with cotton in his ears.
ex2: The school canteen gets so noisy at lunch that Ms D'Souza has to blow a whistle.
note: Noisy describes the place or source; loud describes the sound: a loud horn, a noisy road.

mean: covered with or full of dust
ex: After the long bus ride through Rajasthan, our bags and shoes were dusty and brown.
ex2: Dadi found her old wedding album on a dusty shelf at the back of the storeroom.

mean: cold in an unpleasant way, but not freezing
ex: Delhi mornings get chilly in December, so the newspaper boy wears a monkey cap and gloves.
ex2: The air-conditioned hall was so chilly that guests at the reception wrapped shawls round their shoulders.
note: Do not confuse with 'chilli', the hot pepper. 'A chilly welcome' means an unfriendly one.

mean: having lots of room inside; large
ex: The new flat in Noida is spacious enough for Nani to have her own room with a balcony.
ex2: The spacious new waiting hall at Bhopal station has fans, clean benches and room for hundreds.
note: Use it for rooms, homes and cars, not for open land or people.

mean: having beautiful views of nature
ex: We took the scenic route to Goa along the Konkan coast, with the sea beside us all day.
ex2: The scenic toy train to Darjeeling moves so slowly that boys jump off and climb back on.
note: Say 'scenic beauty', not 'scenery beauty'. Scenery is the noun; scenic describes it.

mean: empty, with no people at all
ex: During the World Cup final, the streets of Kolkata were deserted because everyone was watching the match.
ex2: By eleven at night the Chandigarh market was deserted, and only one dhaba was still frying parathas.
note: Deserted simply means no people are there; 'desolate' adds a feeling of sadness and loneliness.

mean: small, warm and comfortable
ex: Our cosy hostel room in Shimla had two quilts, a heater and a window full of pine trees.
ex2: On rainy evenings the tiny Park Street café feels cosy, with warm lights and fish cutlets on every table.
note: British and Indian spelling is 'cosy'; Americans write 'cozy'.

mean: spreading out widely, often in an untidy way
ex: Bengaluru's sprawling suburbs now cover villages that were growing ragi only twenty years ago.
ex2: The sprawling wedding venue had three lawns, two kitchens and a car park bigger than our whole colony.

mean: dark, dirty and depressing to be in
ex: The coaching centre ran from a dingy basement in Kota with one window and a buzzing tube light.
ex2: After the match we ate at a dingy dhaba near Mohali that served the best rajma chawal in Punjab.
note: Say DIN-jee, with a soft 'j'. 'Dinghy', a small boat, is said DING-ee.

mean: very dry because there has been no rain
ex: After two weak monsoons, the parched fields of Marathwada cracked open like a broken plate.
ex2: After fielding in the Nagpur heat, the parched players emptied ten bottles of water in minutes.
note: Also used for people: 'I'm parched' means very thirsty.

mean: very heavy and fast (used for rain)
ex: Torrential rain flooded the Andheri subway, and schools across Mumbai closed by noon.
ex2: A torrential downpour stopped the Test match at Eden Gardens just when India needed two more wickets.
note: Used almost only for rain; you cannot say 'torrential traffic'.

mean: quiet and hidden, far away from other people
ex: Near Gokarna, the friends found a secluded beach where the only footprints in the sand were crabs'.
ex2: Nanaji built his reading room in a secluded corner of the orchard, far from the noise of the house.
note: Secluded is usually pleasant (private, peaceful); 'isolated' can sound lonely or cut off.

mean: full of people, animals or things moving about
ex: In winter, Chilika Lake is teeming with birds that fly in from Siberia and Central Asia.
ex2: Howrah station was teeming with travellers on the night before Durga Puja began.
note: Usually 'teeming with': the river was teeming with fish.

mean: so hot and airless that it is hard to breathe
ex: The general compartment was stifling, with forty people breathing the same hot air and no fan working.
ex2: Power cuts in a Patna summer make the bedrooms stifling, so the whole family sleeps on the roof.
note: Also used for rules or families that stop you from growing: a stifling atmosphere.

mean: full of twisting paths, like a maze
ex: Without a guide, we got lost in the labyrinthine lanes of old Varanasi between the ghats.
ex2: The labyrinthine corridors of the district court confused Shabana, who asked four lawyers for Room 12.
note: From the labyrinth of Greek myth. Lucknow's Bhool Bhulaiya is a real one.

mean: so light and delicate that it seems not of this world
ex: At dawn, mist rose off the Dal Lake and the shikaras looked ethereal, as if floating on nothing.
ex2: Under the full moon, the white marble of the Taj Mahal looks ethereal, almost ready to float away.
note: Used for light, music and beauty. It sounds poetic, so keep it mostly for writing.
